title: Comparison of generative AI performance on undergraduate and postgraduate written assessments in the biomedical sciences
venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
extended_summary:
This paper examines whether three generative AI tools can produce essays that meet the standards expected in undergraduate and postgraduate biomedical science assessments. The study is motivated by concerns that students may use large language models to draft academic writing, alongside the need for educators to understand what these systems can and cannot do in higher education assessment contexts.

The author prompted ChatGPT 3.5, Google Bard, and Microsoft Bing with essay questions taken from four University College London biomedical science courses spanning UK FHEQ levels 4, 5, 6, and 7. The questions covered topics such as glomerular filtration rate, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, bioinformatics in biomedical research, and the MHC II antigen processing pathway. Each AI-generated essay was anonymized and independently marked by four assessors using criteria aligned to scientific accuracy, mechanistic detail, deviation from topic, context, and coherence. Scores were mapped onto FHEQ level descriptors, and inter-rater reliability was calculated with Kendall’s coefficient of concordance.

Across all levels, ChatGPT generally performed best, followed by Bard and then Bing. The tools were more consistent at postgraduate level than at undergraduate level, but none of them consistently produced strong literature-based examples or reliable references. ChatGPT tended to generate the most coherent, contextually appropriate essays, while Bing was weakest overall, especially in scientific accuracy and narrative quality. The paper concludes that generative AI can produce plausible academic text in biomedical sciences, but it still falls short on depth, precision, and evidentiary support, which limits its suitability as a substitute for student writing and suggests educators should teach students about both the capabilities and limitations of these tools.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI’s conversational large language model chatbot used to generate text from prompts.
identified_tools.use_case: Used to generate 1000-word university-level essay responses to biomedical science questions at UK FHEQ levels 4, 5, 6, and 7, and to attempt reference generation for the level 7 prompt.

findings.finding_summary: Across all four FHEQ levels, ChatGPT scored highest of the three tools on scientific accuracy, mechanistic detail, context, coherence, and total score. Reported total scores were 70.7% (level 4), 70.4% (level 5), 71.85% (level 6), and 69.75% (level 7), with generally high marker agreement on the undergraduate questions.
findings.measure: Marker-rated essay quality across scientific accuracy, mechanistic detail, deviation, context, coherence, and total percentage score

findings.finding_summary: When asked to provide four references for the level 7 response, ChatGPT did not generate direct references and instead stated it could not access external sources and recommended consulting databases or textbooks. The paper reports that none of the models provided appropriate scientific references.
findings.measure: Ability to generate appropriate references on follow-up prompt

identified_tools.name: Gemini
identified_tools.description: Google’s conversational large language model chatbot; the paper refers to Bard, which is Google’s prior product name for Gemini.
identified_tools.use_case: Used to generate 1000-word university-level essay responses to biomedical science questions at UK FHEQ levels 4, 5, 6, and 7, and to attempt reference generation for the level 7 prompt.

findings.finding_summary: Bard/Gemini ranked second overall behind ChatGPT but ahead of Bing across all four FHEQ levels. Total scores were 65.85% (level 4), 64.35% (level 5), 62.05% (level 6), and 66.9% (level 7); the paper characterizes its writing as plausible and coherent but often repetitive and less detailed.
findings.measure: Marker-rated essay quality across scientific accuracy, mechanistic detail, deviation, context, coherence, and total percentage score

findings.finding_summary: On the level 7 follow-up prompt for references, Bard/Gemini returned websites including Wikipedia and other online resources rather than appropriate scientific literature. The paper states that none of the AI models generated appropriate references.
findings.measure: Ability to generate appropriate references on follow-up prompt

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: Generic generative AI / large language model chatbot category with no single named product specified.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper discusses generative AI tools in general as text-generating systems for higher-education essay writing, but its empirical comparison is limited to ChatGPT, Bard/Gemini, and Bing.

findings.finding_summary: The paper concludes that generative AI tools can produce coherent, human-like essay text and often achieve reasonable scientific accuracy, but they are inconsistent in mechanistic detail, context, and reference quality. It also reports that performance differed by model and by FHEQ level, with ChatGPT strongest overall.
findings.measure: Qualitative comparative assessment of generative AI essay output

identified_tools.name: Bing
identified_tools.description: Microsoft’s search-integrated generative AI chatbot, leveraging OpenAI GPT-4 according to the paper.
identified_tools.use_case: Used to generate 1000-word university-level essay responses to biomedical science questions at UK FHEQ levels 4, 5, 6, and 7, and to attempt reference generation for the level 7 prompt.

findings.finding_summary: Bing consistently scored lowest or near-lowest across the four levels, with total scores of 55.75% (level 4), 52.8% (level 5), 55.25% (level 6), and 64.0% (level 7). The paper notes weaker scientific accuracy, mechanistic detail, context, and coherence at UG level, although level 7 performance improved somewhat.
findings.measure: Marker-rated essay quality across scientific accuracy, mechanistic detail, deviation, context, coherence, and total percentage score

findings.finding_summary: On the level 7 follow-up prompt for references, Bing produced entirely fictitious references despite formatting them in conventional citation style. The paper explicitly states that Bing falsified references.
findings.measure: Ability to generate appropriate references on follow-up prompt

quality_tier_rationale: This is a single comparative assessment of AI-generated essay output, not a controlled educational intervention study. It provides descriptive ratings and no causal design, and the evidence is limited to higher-education biomedical science rather than K-12 literacy.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests moderate-to-strong differences in output quality across tools, especially for ChatGPT versus Bing, but it reports no effect sizes and no direct student learning outcomes. The practical impact is mainly on assessment design and AI text quality, not demonstrated educational gain.
